I was not able to search for some tradition-specific sources (Catholic, Orthodox, modern scholarship) due to search limits, but I have strong coverage from the main Protestant traditions through the sources already fetched.

# Ezekiel 29 — Verse-by-Verse Commentary Notes

## OVERVIEW OF THE CHAPTER

**Historical Setting:** Ezekiel 29 opens a four-chapter series of prophecies against Egypt (chs. 29–32). At the time of this first oracle (v.1), Jerusalem was under siege by the Babylonians (2 Kings 25:1–2), and King Zedekiah was pinning his hopes on Egyptian military intervention. The reigning Pharaoh was Hophra (Apries in Greek sources, Jeremiah 44:30). Ezekiel knows that to depend on Egypt is to invite defeat, so he condemns Egypt to show how unacceptable a Judean-Egyptian alliance is in God's sight (cf. 17:15–18; Jeremiah 37:6–10).

**Sources:** Enduring Word (Guzik), Jamieson-Fausset-Brown (JFB), Pulpit Commentary, Gill's Exposition, Matthew Henry, Barnes' Notes, Bridgeway Bible Commentary, Morgan's Exposition.

---

## VERSES 1–3: God Opposes Pharaoh's Pride

**v. 1 — "In the tenth year, on the twelfth day of the tenth month, the word of the LORD came to me…"**

- **The date** corresponds to January/February 587 BC — about a year and two days after Nebuchadnezzar began the siege of Jerusalem (Ezekiel 24:1–2; 2 Kings 25:1), and about seven months before Jerusalem fell. The precision of dating shows each prophecy was called forth by political events. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/); Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **Gill** notes this month is Tebet (part December, part January), and that this prophecy was delivered *before* the one concerning Tyre, though placed *after* it — the arrangement is topical, not chronological. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-29.html)
- **JFB** notes this is "the last of the world kingdoms against which Ezekiel's prophecies are directed, and occupies the largest space … though farther off than Tyre, it exercised a more powerful influence on Israel." — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)

**v. 2 — "Son of man, set your face against Pharaoh king of Egypt and prophesy against him and against all Egypt."**

- **Pharaoh** was a common name for all kings of Egypt, meaning "the sun" (some say "crocodile," which was worshipped in parts of Egypt). The specific Pharaoh was Hophra (Apries), whose reign began prosperously — he took Gaza and Zidon and made himself master of Phoenicia and Palestine, becoming "proudly secure." — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **The prophet's authority:** "The secular historian saw Israel dwarfed into insignificance by mighty neighbours; the religious commentator, the prophet, saw the great powers held firmly in the hand of little Israel's mighty God." (Taylor, cited in Enduring Word) — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)
- **Matthew Henry** notes that Egypt had formerly been a "house of bondage" to God's people but lately had too friendly a correspondence with them, and Israel depended too much upon it. — Matthew Henry (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/mhm/ezekiel-29.html)

**v. 3 — "Behold, I am against you, O Pharaoh king of Egypt, O great monster who lies among his rivers, who says, 'The Nile is mine; I made it myself.'"**

- **"Great monster"** (Hebrew *tannim*): The term refers to a large aquatic creature — specifically the crocodile, which was the emblem of Egypt on Roman coins and was worshipped as the god Sebek. Pharaoh modeled himself after this crocodile-god. — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)
- **"Lies among his rivers"**: Refers to the Nile branches and canals of the Delta, to which Egypt owed its fertility. Pharaoh is pictured lying at ease, rolling in his power and riches. — Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **"The Nile is mine; I made it myself"**: The boast is one of self-deification. The Nile was the source of Egypt's entire existence — without it there would be no Egypt. Pharaoh claims not just ownership but *creation*. "Actually, instead of his making the river, the river made him, for without it the land would have been a desert." (Feinberg) — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)
- **Herodotus** records that Apries "believed himself so firmly established in his kingdom that there was no god that could cast him out of it" — a striking parallel. — Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **Morgan** writes: "It is a graphic method of again drawing attention to the fact that all forgetfulness of God amounts at last to self-deification." — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)

---

## VERSES 4–5: God Will Hook the Crocodile

**v. 4 — "But I will put hooks in your jaws and cause the fish of your streams to cling to your scales…"**

- **Hooks in the jaws**: Herodotus (2.70) describes how Egyptians caught crocodiles by baiting a large hook with swine's flesh. Assyrian sculptures show prisoners with a hook in the underlip, held by a cord from the king. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/); JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **JFB** identifies Amasis as the "hook" who overthrew Hophra. — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **"Fish clinging to scales"**: The adherents of Pharaoh — his soldiers, princes, and people — who would share his fate when he was caught. The fish stuck to the crocodile's horny scales as it was dragged out. — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-29.html)
- **Gill** notes the crocodile's scales were proverbially hard — ancient writers described them as "impenetrable" and "proof against a halberd." The imagery emphasizes Egypt's seemingly invincible strength, which God would easily overcome. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-29.html)

**v. 5 — "I will leave you in the desert … you will fall on the open field and will not be taken away or gathered for burial. I have given you as food to the beasts of the earth and the birds of the air."**

- **The wilderness** represents captivity beyond Egypt's kingdom. JFB suggests a retributive irony: as Egypt once said of Israel "the wilderness hath shut them in" (Exodus 14:3), so Egypt herself would be cast into a wilderness state. — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **Not gathered for burial**: This was a profound disgrace for Egyptians, whose pharaohs were famously diligent in preparing their elaborate tombs and whose culture centered on proper burial. "What a humiliating way to bury a man who claimed to be a god!" (Wiersbe) — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** connects this to the expedition against Cyrene (Herodotus 2.161), where the Egyptian army perished in the deserts west of the Nile, leading to the revolt that installed Amasis. — Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **Gill** notes that the army's carcasses were left unburied — though Pharaoh Hophra himself escaped this particular fate: he was later taken by Amasis and strangled at Sais, then buried among his ancestors. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-29.html)

---

## VERSES 6–7: Egypt, the Broken Reed

**v. 6 — "Then all the people of Egypt will know that I am the LORD. For you were only a staff of reeds to the house of Israel."**

- **"Staff of reed"**: Alludes to the reeds growing on the banks of the Nile — if one leaned on them, they broke. The image echoes 2 Kings 18:21 and Isaiah 36:6, where Rabshakeh himself taunted Hezekiah with the same image. — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm); Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **Matthew Henry** observes that Egypt's sin was to "falsify promise with the Jews, and for this God now punisheth Egypt." — cited in Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)

**v. 7 — "When Israel took hold of you with their hands, you splintered, tearing all their shoulders; when they leaned on you, you broke, and their backs were wrenched."**

- The imagery is vivid: a man leans his full weight on a reed staff, it snaps, the splinters drive into his shoulder and arm, and he falls backward, wrenching his loins. — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)
- This is a reference to Pharaoh Hophra's half-hearted response to Zedekiah's appeal for help during the Babylonian siege (cf. Jeremiah 37:7). It produced only a temporary lull in the siege. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)
- **Gill**: "through Zedekiah's trusting to the king of Egypt, he rebelled against the king of Babylon, which brought on his ruin, and the destruction of his kingdom." — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-29.html)

---

## VERSES 8–12: The Sword, Desolation, and Forty Years

**v. 8 — "Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: I will bring a sword against you and cut off from you man and beast."**

- **"Sword"**: Primarily Nebuchadnezzar's army (v.19). JFB also notes the civil war between Amasis and Hophra. — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **Gill** notes the combination of civil war and foreign invasion: "first a civil war … which issued in the dethroning and strangling of this king … which civil commotions Nebuchadnezzar took the advantage of, and came against Egypt with a large army." — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-29.html)

**v. 9 — "The land of Egypt will become a desolate wasteland. Then they will know that I am the LORD. Because you said, 'The Nile is mine; I made it,'"**

- Note the repetition of Pharaoh's boast from v.3 — God "twits" him with it twice (Trapp). The pride is the stated cause of judgment. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)
- **"Then they will know that I am the LORD"** is a recurring refrain in Ezekiel (cf. the recognition formula). JFB notes it stands "in antithesis to the blasphemous boast." — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)

**v. 10 — "I will turn the land of Egypt into a ruin, a desolate wasteland from Migdol to Syene, and as far as the border of Cush."**

- **"From Migdol to Syene"**: Like "from Dan to Beersheba" in Israel, this defines Egypt from its northern extremity (Migdol, about 12 miles from Pelusium) to its southern (Syene, modern Aswan, on the border of Ethiopia/Cush). — Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **Translation debate**: KJV has "from the tower of Syene," which is misleading. The Hebrew is "from Migdol to Syene." — Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/29.htm); Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-29.html)
- **Gill** discusses Syene extensively: it lay on the border of Ethiopia, was famous for being directly under the tropic of Cancer (no shadow at noon on the summer solstice), and was the place of Juvenal's banishment. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-29.html)

**v. 11 — "No foot of man or beast will pass through, and it will be uninhabited for forty years."**

- **The "forty years"** is one of the most discussed features of this chapter. **There is no known forty-year period of total Egyptian desolation in secular history.**
- **JFB** takes it as an "ideal" forty years: the number forty is "one often connected with affliction and judgment" — the forty days of the Flood, the forty-day fasts of Moses, Elijah, and the Saviour, and the forty years of Israel's wilderness wandering. The interval between Egypt's overthrow by Nebuchadnezzar and deliverance by Cyrus was *about* forty years. He holds it means "a wilderness state of social and political degradation, rather than a literal non-passing of man or beast." — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** agrees: "It need hardly be said that history reveals no such period of devastation. Nor, indeed, would anything but the most prosaic literalism justify us in looking for it. We are dealing with the language of a poet-prophet, which is naturally that of hyperbole." — Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **Feinberg** (cited in Enduring Word) takes the opposite view: "Because no such forty-year period is known in Egyptian history, some claim a literal fulfillment of the prophecy was never intended … But there is nothing in the context that would indicate a shift from the literal to the figurative." — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)
- **Barnes' Notes** states: "No great stress is to be laid on the exact number of years. The number of years passed in the wilderness became to the Hebrews a significant period of chastisement." — Barnes (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **Gill** notes a Jewish tradition connecting the forty years to the supposed forty-two years of famine in Pharaoh's dream: because only two years of famine occurred, Egypt would lie waste for forty years as a substitute. He also calculates that from Nebuchadnezzar's destruction of Egypt to Cyrus's conquest of Babylon was about forty (or forty-three) years. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-29.html)

**v. 12 — "I will make the land of Egypt a desolation among desolate lands … And I will disperse the Egyptians among the nations and scatter them throughout the countries."**

- **Fairbairn** (Presbyterian) sees a parallel: "As Israel passed through a term of wilderness discipline … which was in its essential features to be repeated again, so it was to be with Egypt." — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **"Scatter … disperse"**: Some were carried to Babylon (Berosus, the Babylonian historian, states Nebuchadnezzar took great numbers of captives to Babylon); others fled to Arabia and Ethiopia. But mainly the "scattering" was the dissipation of their power. — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm); Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** notes that "records are silent as to any such dispersion," but such deportation was the uniform sequel of Oriental conquests — as with the captivities of Samaria and Jerusalem. — Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/29.htm)

---

## VERSES 13–16: Restoration — A Lowly Kingdom

**v. 13 — "For this is what the Lord GOD says: At the end of forty years I will gather the Egyptians from the nations to which they were scattered."**

- This is the **only place in Ezekiel** where a non-Israelite nation receives a promise of restoration. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)
- **Gill** suggests Cyrus, who proclaimed liberty to the Jews, probably also stirred up liberty for the Egyptians to return. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-29.html)
- **JFB** references Jeremiah 46:26 which also promises Egypt's restoration. — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)

**v. 14 — "I will restore Egypt from captivity and bring them back to the land of Pathros, the land of their origin. There they will be a lowly kingdom."**

- **Pathros** = Upper Egypt (the Thebaid), the oldest part of Egyptian civilization; "the land of their birth/origin." — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm); Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **"Lowly kingdom"** (KJV "base kingdom"): Under Amasis, Egypt became dependent on Babylon; it was humbled further under Cambyses (Persian conquest). Though it rose somewhat under the Ptolemies, it never regained its ancient pre-eminence as an independent world power. — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)

**v. 15 — "Egypt will be the lowliest of kingdoms and will never again exalt itself above the nations. For I will diminish Egypt so that it will never again rule over the nations."**

- **History confirms** this well: after the Babylonian and Persian conquests, Egypt passed under Greek (Ptolemaic) rule, then Roman, then Saracen, then Mamluk, then Ottoman. "From the time of Herodotus the kingdom never again became really independent." — Barnes (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **The Pulpit Commentary** observes that the Ptolemies were an *alien* dynasty; "the nationality of Egypt was suppressed, and Alexandria, practically a Greek city, took the place of Memphis, Sais, and Thebes." — Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **Gill** traces Egypt's decline through Persian domination, Alexander's conquest, Ptolemaic rule, Roman province status (600–700 years), Saracen conquest, Mamluk usurpation, and finally Turkish annexation (1517) — showing Egypt as perpetually ruled by foreigners. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-29.html)

**v. 16 — "Egypt will never again be an object of trust for the house of Israel, but will remind them of their iniquity in turning to the Egyptians. Then they will know that I am the Lord GOD."**

- One purpose of Egypt's reduction was to remove the temptation for Israel to trust in Egypt rather than in God. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)
- **JFB**: "Egypt, when restored, shall be so circumscribed in power that it shall be no longer an object of confidence to Israel, as formerly." — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **The phrase "brings their iniquity to remembrance"**: JFB (following Henderson) renders it: "while they (the Israelites) look to (or turn after) them" — Israel's looking to Egypt rather than God causes their iniquity to be remembered by God. — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **Ellicott** adds: "The result of this judgment in God's providence concerning His people is brought out: they had hitherto continually transgressed by looking to Egypt for aid; now this temptation should be entirely removed." — Ellicott (from search excerpt, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-29.html)

---

## VERSES 17–18: The Later Oracle — Nebuchadnezzar's Unrewarded Labor at Tyre

**v. 17 — "In the twenty-seventh year, on the first day of the first month, the word of the LORD came to me…"**

- This is the **latest dated prophecy** in Ezekiel (571 BC), about seventeen years after the preceding oracle (vv.1–16), and even later than the vision of chapters 40–48 (cf. 40:1). — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)
- **Pulpit Commentary**: The date (first day of the year) "is not without significance. Then, as now, the beginning of a new year was a time for men generally to look before and after, for a prophet to ask himself what new stage in the order of the Divine government the year was likely to produce." — Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **Clarke** notes this is "fifteen years after the taking of Jerusalem … and it is supposed to be the last which this prophet wrote." — cited in Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)
- This oracle is placed out of chronological order (the next dated oracle in 30:20 is earlier) to maintain topical unity. — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)

**v. 18 — "Son of man, Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon caused his army to labor strenuously against Tyre. Every head was made bald and every shoulder made raw. But he and his army received no wages from Tyre…"**

- **The thirteen-year siege**: Josephus (Antiquities x.11.1) states the Babylonian siege of Tyre lasted thirteen years. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)
- **"Every head made bald, every shoulder rubbed raw"**: These were not battle wounds but the effects of carrying vast amounts of dirt and stones to construct siege mounds and ramps — and perhaps an unsuccessful attempt to build a causeway to the island fortress. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/); JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **Jerome** (cited in Pulpit Commentary) states the labors consisted mainly in attempting to fill up the strait between the island-city and the mainland with masses of stone and rubbish, carried on heads and shoulders. — Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **"No wages"**: The Tyrians, finding they could not defend the city, loaded their wealth onto ships and escaped (to Carthage, per Clarke). So Nebuchadnezzar lost the spoil of one of the richest cities in the world. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/); Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **Important nuance**: Some commentators (Alexander, cited in Enduring Word) push back against claims that this proves Ezekiel's earlier prophecies against Tyre failed. "The Scriptures do not demand that complete fulfillment lay in this one siege alone." — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)

---

## VERSES 19–20: Egypt as Nebuchadnezzar's Wages

**v. 19 — "Therefore this is what the Lord GOD says: I will give the land of Egypt to Nebuchadnezzar king of Babylon, who will carry off its wealth, seize its spoil, and remove its plunder. This will be the wages for his army."**

- God compensates Nebuchadnezzar for his disappointing Tyrian campaign by giving him the spoil of Egypt. — Bridgeway Bible Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/ezekiel-29.html)
- **Historical evidence**: A fragmentary cuneiform text (B.M. 33041) implies Babylonia invaded Egypt around 568/567 BC, corroborated by Josephus (Antiquities X, 180–82). This was within three years of this prophecy. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)
- **JFB** notes: "he shall take her multitude" means a multitude of captives (not just "store" as Fairbairn had it). — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)
- The play on words: "spoil her spoil, prey her prey" — as Egypt had spoiled other nations, so she would be spoiled. — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)

**v. 20 — "I have given him the land of Egypt as the reward for his labor, because it was done for Me, declares the Lord GOD."**

- **"Because they wrought for Me"**: A remarkable statement. The pagan Babylonian army, entirely unaware of it, was serving God's purposes as His instrument of judgment on Tyre (cf. Jeremiah 25:9 where Nebuchadnezzar is called "My servant"). Therefore God, as their true Employer, ensured they received fitting wages. — Bridgeway Bible Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/ezekiel-29.html); JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **F.B. Meyer** (cited in Enduring Word) draws an application for Christian workers: "If He gave Egypt to a heathen king for his service in respect to Tyre, we may also expect Him to bestow a reward on those who have built gold, silver, and precious stones, into His holy temple." — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)
- **Matthew Henry** summarizes the theological point: "In both cases they were 'hired' by God to carry out his judgment, and he would make sure they received fitting 'wages.'" — Bridgeway Bible Commentary (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/ezekiel-29.html)

---

## VERSE 21: A Horn for Israel, an Open Mouth for Ezekiel

**v. 21 — "In that day I will cause a horn to sprout for the house of Israel, and I will open your mouth to speak among them. Then they will know that I am the LORD."**

- **"Horn"**: The symbol of power and strength (cf. 1 Samuel 2:1; Psalm 92:10; 132:17). Israel's horn had been cut off; now it would begin to sprout again. — Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/29.htm)

**On the "horn" — Messianic or national restoration?**

- **JFB** sees a Messianic dimension: "I will cause its ancient glory to revive: an earnest of Israel's full glory under Messiah, the son of David (Luke 1:69). Even in Babylon an earnest was given of this in Daniel (Da 6:2) and Jeconiah (Jer 52:31)." — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **Enduring Word** (Guzik) leans non-Messianic: "Psalm 132:17 also makes mention of the horn of the house of Israel: 'There I will make the horn of David grow.' Yet the context here seems to be more the restoration of Israel than the emergence of the Messiah." Alexander (cited there) says: "No Messiah — or any other ruler — came in Israel around 586 B.C. The symbol must refer to the strength and encouragement that Israel was to receive when she observed God's faithfulness to execute his judgment on her enemy, Egypt." — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)
- **Wiersbe** (cited in Enduring Word): "The prophet added a word of promise for the Jews … assuring them that there would come for them a time of restoration when He would give them new strength (the budding horn) for their new challenges." — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)
- **Ellicott** sees both immediate and eschatological significance: "The prophet speaks of this as only in germ, but looking on to its further development, under the figure of making a horn to bud forth … Israel's reviving prosperity should date from the destruction of its trust in earthly aid." — Ellicott (from search excerpt, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-29.html)

- **"I will open your mouth to speak among them"**: Ezekiel had apparently been largely silent since the fall of Jerusalem and the vision of the restored temple. Now, with the fulfillment of his prophecies against Egypt, his credibility would be restored. "This seems to mean that the skepticism of the captives regarding Ezekiel would be removed and they would come to regard him as a true prophet." (Smith) — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/); Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **JFB** connects this to Ezekiel 24:27: "When thy predictions shall have come to pass, thy words henceforth shall be more heeded." — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **JFB's summary of the chapter's theological arc**: "In the evil only, not in the good, was Egypt to be parallel to Israel. The very downfall of Egypt will be the signal for the rise of Israel, because of God's covenant with the latter." — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)

---

## POINTS OF TRADITIONAL DIFFERENCE AMONG PROTESTANT TRADITIONS

### 1. The Forty Years — Literal or Figurative? (vv. 11–12)

- **Reformed/Amillennial-leaning (JFB, Fairbairn, Pulpit Commentary)**: The forty years is an "ideal" or "symbolic" number denoting a period of chastisement and degradation, not a mathematically precise forty years. JFB explicitly says "the ideal forty years' wilderness state … rather than a literal non-passing of man or beast for that term, is mainly intended." — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **Dispensational/Literal-leaning (Feinberg, cited by Guzik/Enduring Word)**: "Because no such forty-year period is known in Egyptian history, some claim a literal fulfillment … was never intended … But there is nothing in the context that would indicate a shift from the literal to the figurative." This represents the view that the forty years must have happened historically even if the record is yet undiscovered. — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)
- **Baptist (Gill)**: Gill reports the Jewish tradition connecting it to the years of famine in Pharaoh's dream, and also calculates the approximate forty (or forty-three) years from Nebuchadnezzar's conquest to Cyrus's decree — suggesting a possible historical fit without committing to a strict literalist or figurative reading. — Gill (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/geb/ezekiel-29.html)

### 2. The "Horn of the House of Israel" (v. 21) — Messianic or National?

- **Reformed/Presbyterian (JFB)**: Explicitly Messianic. The horn is "an earnest of Israel's full glory under Messiah, the son of David (Luke 1:69)." — JFB (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/jfb/ezekiel/29.htm)
- **Anglican (Ellicott)**: Sees both an immediate fulfillment and a developing "germ" that looks forward to fuller development — a both/and approach. — Ellicott (from search excerpt, https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/ebc/ezekiel-29.html)
- **Dispensational/Pentecostal-leaning (Enduring Word/Guzik citing Alexander)**: Non-Messianic in the immediate context. The horn is "the strength and encouragement that Israel was to receive when she observed God's faithfulness to execute his judgment on her enemy, Egypt, in accord … with the Abrahamic covenant (Genesis 12:3)." — Enduring Word (https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/ezekiel-29/)
- **Pulpit Commentary (Anglican)**: Quietly wonders whether Ezekiel, in his later years, was "watching the growth of Salathiel or Zerubbabel?" — suggesting hope in the Davidic line, but not pressing a direct Messianic reading. — Pulpit Commentary (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/pulpit/ezekiel/29.htm)

### 3. The "Dragon/Monster" — Crocodile or Mythological Symbol? (v. 3)

- **All traditional Protestant commentators consulted** identify it as the crocodile, the natural symbol of Egypt, worshipped as the god Sebek. — JFB, Pulpit, Gill, Enduring Word (all agree)
- **Bridgeway Bible Commentary** uses the phrase "mythical monster," acknowledging the symbolic dimension while retaining the crocodile identification. — Bridgeway (https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/bbc/ezekiel-29.html)
- **No sharp tradition divide** here—the crocodile identification is broadly shared from Baptist (Gill) through Reformed (JFB) to Pentecostal (Guzik).

### 4. Application Emphasis Varies by Tradition

- **Reformed (JFB)**: Emphasizes God's sovereignty over pagan nations — Nebuchadnezzar works for God unwittingly; Egypt's fall parallels Israel's discipline.
- **Baptist (Gill)**: Provides extensive historical and geographical detail, reflecting the Baptist tradition's high view of Scripture's factual accuracy.
- **Pentecostal/Charismatic (Enduring Word/Guzik)**: Emphasizes personal application — "When we put our trust in human power and earthly strength instead of God, we are left disappointed and weakened." Also highlights the unique mercy shown to a Gentile nation (v.13).
- **Matthew Henry (Puritan/Evangelical)**: Draws the moral lesson: "God, not only in justice, but in wisdom and goodness to us, breaks the creature-stays on which we lean, that they may be no more our confidence." — Matthew Henry (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/mhc/ezekiel/29.htm)

## NOTE ON OTHER VIEWS

I was unable to conduct additional searches for Catholic, Orthodox, or modern scholarly perspectives due to search limits. However, from the sources already consulted:

- **Catholic/Orthodox**: No distinctively Catholic or Orthodox commentaries were accessed in these searches.
- **Modern scholarship**: The Pulpit Commentary occasionally interacts with Herodotus and classical sources. Feinberg and Block (cited in Enduring Word) represent more recent evangelical scholarship.
- **Barnes' Notes** represents a mediating view: acknowledging that the "forty years" should not be pressed literally, while affirming that Nebuchadnezzar's ravages were "the beginning of the end" and that the cumulative decline under Persians, Greeks, and Romans fulfilled the prophecy amply. — Barnes (https://biblehub.com/commentaries/barnes/ezekiel/29.htm)
